claim: Paternal nicotine exposure prior to reproduction induced a broad protective response to multiple xenobiotics in male offspring.
source: Paternal exposure to nicotine prior to reproduction induced a broad protective response to multiple xenobiotics in male offspring.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental results including survival assays with nicotine and cocaine, hepatic gene expression changes, and enhanced drug clearance measurements.

claim: Paternal nicotine exposure increased survival of male offspring following injection of toxic levels of nicotine.
source: This effect manifested as increased survival following injection of toxic levels of either nicotine or cocaine, accompanied by hepatic upregulation of xenobiotic processing genes, and enhanced drug clearance.
evidence: Demonstrated by survival curves in self-administration and single-dose challenge experiments.

claim: Paternal nicotine exposure increased survival of male offspring following injection of toxic levels of cocaine.
source: This effect manifested as increased survival following injection of toxic levels of either nicotine or cocaine, accompanied by hepatic upregulation of xenobiotic processing genes, and enhanced drug clearance.
evidence: Demonstrated by cocaine toxicity assays showing enhanced survival in NIC offspring.

claim: Paternal nicotine exposure resulted in hepatic upregulation of xenobiotic processing genes in offspring.
source: This effect manifested as increased survival following injection of toxic levels of either nicotine or cocaine, accompanied by hepatic upregulation of xenobiotic processing genes, and enhanced drug clearance.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data from isolated hepatocytes showing upregulation of Phase I, II, and III detoxification genes.

claim: Paternal nicotine exposure enhanced drug clearance in offspring.
source: This effect manifested as increased survival following injection of toxic levels of either nicotine or cocaine, accompanied by hepatic upregulation of xenobiotic processing genes, and enhanced drug clearance.
evidence: Demonstrated by elevated cotinine levels at early time points after nicotine injection, indicating faster nicotine metabolism.

claim: The protective effect of paternal nicotine exposure could be induced by a nicotinic receptor antagonist.
source: Surprisingly, this protective effect could also be induced by a nicotinic receptor antagonist, suggesting that xenobiotic exposure, rather than nicotinic receptor signaling, is responsible for programming offspring drug resistance.
evidence: Demonstrated by mecamylamine experiments showing similar protective effects in offspring.

claim: Xenobiotic exposure, rather than nicotinic receptor signaling, is responsible for programming offspring drug resistance.
source: Surprisingly, this protective effect could also be induced by a nicotinic receptor antagonist, suggesting that xenobiotic exposure, rather than nicotinic receptor signaling, is responsible for programming offspring drug resistance.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that both nicotine (agonist) and mecamylamine (antagonist) induce similar protective effects.

claim: Paternal drug exposure induces a protective phenotype in offspring by enhancing metabolic tolerance to xenobiotics.
source: Thus, paternal drug exposure induces a protective phenotype in offspring by enhancing metabolic tolerance to xenobiotics.
evidence: Supported by enhanced drug clearance, upregulation of xenobiotic processing genes, and protection from hepatotoxicity.

claim: Maternal use of nicotine has been linked to multiple phenotypes in offspring.
source: Maternal use of nicotine has been linked to multiple phenotypes in offspring (Yohn et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2014), and although effects of paternal nicotine exposure have been less-studied, paternal smoking in humans has been suggested to affect metabolic phenotypes in children (Pembrey et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Paternal smoking in humans has been suggested to affect metabolic phenotypes in children.
source: Maternal use of nicotine has been linked to multiple phenotypes in offspring (Yohn et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2014), and although effects of paternal nicotine exposure have been less-studied, paternal smoking in humans has been suggested to affect metabolic phenotypes in children (Pembrey et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pembrey et al., 2006.

claim: Male mice consumed nicotine or control solutions from 3 weeks of age until 8 weeks of age.
source: Mice consumed nicotine or control solutions (NIC or TA, respectively) from 3 weeks of age until 8 weeks of age.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol used.

claim: The nicotine administration regimen maintains a high level of nicotine in the bloodstream.
source: As previously described (Zhao-Shea et al., 2015), this administration regimen maintains a high level of nicotine in the bloodstream (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B), and results in nicotine dependence in exposed animals (Zhao-Shea et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B showing cotinine levels.

claim: The nicotine administration regimen results in nicotine dependence in exposed animals.
source: As previously described (Zhao-Shea et al., 2015), this administration regimen maintains a high level of nicotine in the bloodstream (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B), and results in nicotine dependence in exposed animals (Zhao-Shea et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhao-Shea et al., 2013.

claim: Males were withdrawn from nicotine for one week prior to mating to prevent seminal fluid transmission of nicotine.
source: Males were then withdrawn from nicotine for one week prior to mating in order to prevent any potential for seminal fluid transmission of nicotine (the half-life of nicotine in mice is ~10 min, the half-life of its 'long-lived' metabolite cotinine is ~40 min [Siu and Tyndale, 2007]).
evidence: This is an experimental design decision supported by knowledge of nicotine pharmacokinetics.

claim: The half-life of nicotine in mice is approximately 10 minutes.
source: Males were then withdrawn from nicotine for one week prior to mating in order to prevent any potential for seminal fluid transmission of nicotine (the half-life of nicotine in mice is ~10 min, the half-life of its 'long-lived' metabolite cotinine is ~40 min [Siu and Tyndale, 2007]).
evidence: Supported by citation to Siu and Tyndale, 2007.

claim: The half-life of cotinine in mice is approximately 40 minutes.
source: Males were then withdrawn from nicotine for one week prior to mating in order to prevent any potential for seminal fluid transmission of nicotine (the half-life of nicotine in mice is ~10 min, the half-life of its 'long-lived' metabolite cotinine is ~40 min [Siu and Tyndale, 2007]).
evidence: Supported by citation to Siu and Tyndale, 2007.

claim: There was no difference in average litter size between control and nicotine matings.
source: Overall, we observed no difference in average size or sex ratio of litters arising from control or nicotine matings, or in offspring body weights (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There was no difference in sex ratio of litters between control and nicotine matings.
source: Overall, we observed no difference in average size or sex ratio of litters arising from control or nicotine matings, or in offspring body weights (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: There was no difference in offspring body weights between control and nicotine matings.
source: Overall, we observed no difference in average size or sex ratio of litters arising from control or nicotine matings, or in offspring body weights (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–F.

claim: There were no differences between TA and NIC offspring in time spent in the center during an open field anxiety test.
source: Importantly, we observed no differences between TA and NIC offspring in time spent in the center during an open field anxiety test, or in time spent or number of entries into the open arms of an elevated plus maze (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There were no differences between TA and NIC offspring in time spent in the open arms of an elevated plus maze.
source: Importantly, we observed no differences between TA and NIC offspring in time spent in the center during an open field anxiety test, or in time spent or number of entries into the open arms of an elevated plus maze (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There were no differences between TA and NIC offspring in number of entries into the open arms of an elevated plus maze.
source: Importantly, we observed no differences between TA and NIC offspring in time spent in the center during an open field anxiety test, or in time spent or number of entries into the open arms of an elevated plus maze (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The nicotine administration paradigm does not induce a stress response robustly enough to affect offspring phenotype.
source: These results and results discussed below (see Figure 6) indicate that our nicotine administration paradigm does not induce a stress response robustly enough, or for long enough prior to mating, to affect offspring phenotype.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of anxiety-related behavioral changes and mecamylamine experiments.

claim: There was no significant difference in nicotine sensitivity between TA and NIC male offspring in the locomotor suppression assay.
source: Using this assay, we observed no significant difference in nicotine sensitivity between TA and NIC offspring, either for male or female offspring (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity data shown in Figure 1.

claim: There was no significant difference in nicotine sensitivity between TA and NIC female offspring in the locomotor suppression assay.
source: Using this assay, we observed no significant difference in nicotine sensitivity between TA and NIC offspring, either for male or female offspring (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The acute locomotor suppression response to nicotine is not altered by paternal nicotine exposure.
source: We therefore conclude that the acute locomotor suppression response to nicotine is not altered by our paternal nicotine exposure paradigm.
evidence: Concluded from the lack of differences in locomotor activity assays.

claim: There was no difference in daily nicotine self-administration between offspring of control males and offspring of nicotine-exposed males.
source: Overall, there was no difference in daily nicotine SA between offspring of control males and offspring of nicotine-exposed males (Figure 2A), indicating that nicotine reward behavior is not significantly reprogrammed by our paternal exposure paradigm.
evidence: Supported by self-administration data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Nicotine reward behavior is not significantly reprogrammed by paternal nicotine exposure.
source: Overall, there was no difference in daily nicotine SA between offspring of control males and offspring of nicotine-exposed males (Figure 2A), indicating that nicotine reward behavior is not significantly reprogrammed by our paternal exposure paradigm.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of differences in self-administration behavior.

claim: NIC offspring survived for many more days on average than TA offspring during the escalating nicotine dosing schedule.
source: We found that in our strain background, the escalating nicotine dosing schedule of SA resulted in death of nearly all animals tested at the highest doses used. Surprisingly, NIC offspring survived for many more days, on average, than TA offspring (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The difference in survival between TA and NIC offspring during self-administration was highly significant (p<0.0001).
source: This difference in survival was highly significant (Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon p<0.0001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of survival data.

claim: Paternal nicotine exposure can protect offspring from nicotine toxicity.
source: As there was no difference in the daily levels of nicotine administered by either group (Figure 2A), this result suggests that paternal nicotine exposure can protect offspring from nicotine toxicity.
evidence: Inferred from enhanced survival despite similar nicotine consumption.

claim: Naïve TA and NIC offspring exhibited no significant difference in susceptibility to a toxic nicotine injection.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, naïve TA and NIC offspring exhibited no significant difference in susceptibility to a toxic nicotine injection, indicating that paternal nicotine exposure does not program a constitutively nicotine-resistant state.
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Paternal nicotine exposure does not program a constitutively nicotine-resistant state.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, naïve TA and NIC offspring exhibited no significant difference in susceptibility to a toxic nicotine injection, indicating that paternal nicotine exposure does not program a constitutively nicotine-resistant state.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of protection in naïve animals.

claim: Male offspring of nicotine-exposed fathers became significantly more tolerant to a lethal nicotine challenge than control offspring after chronic nicotine acclimation.
source: In contrast, and consistent with the results of the self-administration test, male (but not female) offspring of nicotine-exposed fathers became significantly more tolerant to a lethal nicotine challenge than control offspring (Figure 3B), but only once they had become acclimated to a week of chronic nicotine.
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Female offspring of nicotine-exposed fathers did not become more tolerant to a lethal nicotine challenge after chronic nicotine acclimation.
source: In contrast, and consistent with the results of the self-administration test, male (but not female) offspring of nicotine-exposed fathers became significantly more tolerant to a lethal nicotine challenge than control offspring (Figure 3B), but only once they had become acclimated to a week of chronic nicotine.
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Male offspring of nicotine-exposed fathers exhibit an enhanced ability to develop tolerance to toxic doses of nicotine.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that male offspring of nicotine-exposed fathers exhibit an enhanced ability to develop tolerance to toxic doses of nicotine, but that this tolerance is only revealed following prior exposure to sub-lethal levels of nicotine.
evidence: Concluded from the combination of naïve and chronic nicotine challenge experiments.

claim: The enhanced tolerance to nicotine in NIC offspring is only revealed following prior exposure to sub-lethal levels of nicotine.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that male offspring of nicotine-exposed fathers exhibit an enhanced ability to develop tolerance to toxic doses of nicotine, but that this tolerance is only revealed following prior exposure to sub-lethal levels of nicotine.
evidence: Concluded from the difference between naïve and chronic challenge experiments.

claim: Nicotine-acclimated NIC offspring exhibit significantly higher levels of cotinine at earlier time points after nicotine injection than TA offspring.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, nicotine-acclimated NIC offspring exhibit significantly higher levels of the long-lived nicotine metabolite cotinine at earlier time points after nicotine injection than do TA offspring.
evidence: Supported by cotinine measurement data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Enhanced nicotine clearance underlies the nicotine resistance phenotype displayed by NIC offspring.
source: This finding is consistent with enhanced nicotine clearance underlying the nicotine resistance phenotype displayed by these animals, suggesting that paternal nicotine exposure programs a state of enhanced metabolic tolerance in offspring.
evidence: Inferred from the elevated cotinine levels indicating faster metabolism.

claim: Paternal nicotine exposure programs a state of enhanced metabolic tolerance in offspring.
source: This finding is consistent with enhanced nicotine clearance underlying the nicotine resistance phenotype displayed by these animals, suggesting that paternal nicotine exposure programs a state of enhanced metabolic tolerance in offspring.
evidence: Inferred from enhanced drug clearance and upregulation of metabolic genes.

claim: Paternal nicotine exposure significantly affected the expression levels of 51 genes in hepatocytes.
source: Paternal nicotine exposure significantly (adjusted p<0.05) affected the expression levels of 51 genes, with upregulated genes being significantly enriched for those involved in lipid metabolism (p=3.9e-14), amino acid catabolism (p=6.6e-8), and various mitochondrial annotations including mitochondrial membrane (p=1.9e-7) (Figure 4D–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data from hepatocytes.

claim: Genes upregulated in NIC hepatocytes were significantly enriched for those involved in lipid metabolism.
source: Paternal nicotine exposure significantly (adjusted p<0.05) affected the expression levels of 51 genes, with upregulated genes being significantly enriched for those involved in lipid metabolism (p=3.9e-14), amino acid catabolism (p=6.6e-8), and various mitochondrial annotations including mitochondrial membrane (p=1.9e-7) (Figure 4D–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: Genes upregulated in NIC hepatocytes were significantly enriched for those involved in amino acid catabolism.
source: Paternal nicotine exposure significantly (adjusted p<0.05) affected the expression levels of 51 genes, with upregulated genes being significantly enriched for those involved in lipid metabolism (p=3.9e-14), amino acid catabolism (p=6.6e-8), and various mitochondrial annotations including mitochondrial membrane (p=1.9e-7) (Figure 4D–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: Genes upregulated in NIC hepatocytes were significantly enriched for mitochondrial annotations.
source: Paternal nicotine exposure significantly (adjusted p<0.05) affected the expression levels of 51 genes, with upregulated genes being significantly enriched for those involved in lipid metabolism (p=3.9e-14), amino acid catabolism (p=6.6e-8), and various mitochondrial annotations including mitochondrial membrane (p=1.9e-7) (Figure 4D–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: NIC hepatocytes exhibited increased expression of genes involved in drug metabolism.
source: Most notably, given the nicotine resistance observed at the organismal level, NIC hepatocytes also exhibited increased expression of genes involved in drug metabolism (p=4.3e-6), with upregulated genes including 'Phase I' (Cyp1a2, Cyp2c68) and 'Phase II' (Ugt2a3, Ugt2b1, Sult1d1, and Sult1a1) detoxification enzymes, 'Phase III' membrane transporters (Slco1a4), as well as genes encoding the xenobiotic-responsive nuclear hormone receptors CAR and PXR (Nr1h3 and Nr1i2) (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data from hepatocytes.

claim: NIC hepatocytes exhibited upregulation of Phase I detoxification enzymes including Cyp1a2 and Cyp2c68.
source: Most notably, given the nicotine resistance observed at the organismal level, NIC hepatocytes also exhibited increased expression of genes involved in drug metabolism (p=4.3e-6), with upregulated genes including 'Phase I' (Cyp1a2, Cyp2c68) and 'Phase II' (Ugt2a3, Ugt2b1, Sult1d1, and Sult1a1) detoxification enzymes, 'Phase III' membrane transporters (Slco1a4), as well as genes encoding the xenobiotic-responsive nuclear hormone receptors CAR and PXR (Nr1h3 and Nr1i2) (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data from hepatocytes.

claim: NIC hepatocytes exhibited upregulation of Phase II detoxification enzymes including Ugt2a3, Ugt2b1, Sult1d1, and Sult1a1.
source: Most notably, given the nicotine resistance observed at the organismal level, NIC hepatocytes also exhibited increased expression of genes involved in drug metabolism (p=4.3e-6), with upregulated genes including 'Phase I' (Cyp1a2, Cyp2c68) and 'Phase II' (Ugt2a3, Ugt2b1, Sult1d1, and Sult1a1) detoxification enzymes, 'Phase III' membrane transporters (Slco1a4), as well as genes encoding the xenobiotic-responsive nuclear hormone receptors CAR and PXR (Nr1h3 and Nr1i2) (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data from hepatocytes.

claim: NIC hepatocytes exhibited upregulation of Phase III membrane transporters including Slco1a4.
source: Most notably, given the nicotine resistance observed at the organismal level, NIC hepatocytes also exhibited increased expression of genes involved in drug metabolism (p=4.3e-6), with upregulated genes including 'Phase I' (Cyp1a2, Cyp2c68) and 'Phase II' (Ugt2a3, Ugt2b1, Sult1d1, and Sult1a1) detoxification enzymes, 'Phase III' membrane transporters (Slco1a4), as well as genes encoding the xenobiotic-responsive nuclear hormone receptors CAR and PXR (Nr1h3 and Nr1i2) (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data from hepatocytes.

claim: NIC hepatocytes exhibited upregulation of genes encoding the xenobiotic-responsive nuclear hormone receptors CAR and PXR.
source: Most notably, given the nicotine resistance observed at the organismal level, NIC hepatocytes also exhibited increased expression of genes involved in drug metabolism (p=4.3e-6), with upregulated genes including 'Phase I' (Cyp1a2, Cyp2c68) and 'Phase II' (Ugt2a3, Ugt2b1, Sult1d1, and Sult1a1) detoxification enzymes, 'Phase III' membrane transporters (Slco1a4), as well as genes encoding the xenobiotic-responsive nuclear hormone receptors CAR and PXR (Nr1h3 and Nr1i2) (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data from hepatocytes.

claim: Cyp2a5 was upregulated approximately 2-fold on average in NIC hepatocytes.
source: In addition, the primary cytochrome involved in nicotine clearance in rodents, Cyp2a5, was upregulated ~2 fold on average in NIC hepatocytes.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq and q-RT-PCR data.

claim: Cyp2a5 is the primary cytochrome involved in nicotine clearance in rodents.
source: In addition, the primary cytochrome involved in nicotine clearance in rodents, Cyp2a5, was upregulated ~2 fold on average in NIC hepatocytes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nicotine metabolism in rodents.

claim: NIC hepatocytes exhibit a general derepression of target genes for a broad range of nuclear hormone receptors.
source: These gene expression studies thus reveal that, relative to TA hepatocytes, NIC hepatocytes exhibit a general derepression of target genes for a broad range of nuclear hormone receptors.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of gene expression changes observed in RNA-Seq data.

claim: 1861 peaks of chromatin accessibility differ significantly between TA and NIC hepatocytes.
source: Whatever the basis for this global change in chromatin accessibility, we additionally identified 1861 peaks of chromatin accessibility (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 3D–H, Supplementary file 3) that differ significantly between TA and NIC hepatocytes after correcting for the global difference in peak height between these samples.
evidence: Supported by ATAC-Seq data analysis.

claim: Differentially accessible chromatin peaks were significantly enriched near genes involved in lipid metabolism.
source: Consistent with the changes in mRNA abundance observed in hepatocytes, these peaks were significantly enriched near genes involved in lipid metabolism (p=2.8e-18) and xenobiotic metabolism (p=1.3e-6), along with many related GO categories.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis of ATAC-Seq peaks.

claim: Differentially accessible chromatin peaks were significantly enriched near genes involved in xenobiotic metabolism.
source: Consistent with the changes in mRNA abundance observed in hepatocytes, these peaks were significantly enriched near genes involved in lipid metabolism (p=2.8e-18) and xenobiotic metabolism (p=1.3e-6), along with many related GO categories.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis of ATAC-Seq peaks.

claim: A history of paternal drug exposure can influence the chromatin landscape of hepatocytes in offspring.
source: We conclude that a history of paternal drug exposure can influence the chromatin landscape of hepatocytes in offspring, resulting in a broad increase in accessibility at regulatory elements involved in metabolism and detoxification.
evidence: Concluded from ATAC-Seq data showing differential chromatin accessibility.

claim: Paternal drug exposure results in a broad increase in chromatin accessibility at regulatory elements involved in metabolism and detoxification in offspring hepatocytes.
source: We conclude that a history of paternal drug exposure can influence the chromatin landscape of hepatocytes in offspring, resulting in a broad increase in accessibility at regulatory elements involved in metabolism and detoxification.
evidence: Concluded from ATAC-Seq data analysis.

claim: Naïve NIC and TA animals did not exhibit significant differences in their resistance to cocaine toxicity.
source: We first assessed cocaine toxicity in 'naïve' animals that had not been previously directly exposed to nicotine or cocaine. Similar to our findings with nicotine toxicity (Figure 3A), naïve NIC and TA animals did not exhibit significant differences in their resistance to cocaine toxicity (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by cocaine toxicity data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Acclimation of NIC offspring to cocaine resulted in enhanced resistance to cocaine toxicity relative to TA controls.
source: Astonishingly, this acclimation protocol resulted in enhanced resistance to cocaine toxicity in NIC offspring, relative to TA controls (Figure 5B), revealing that NIC offspring are hyper-responsive to multiple xenobiotics.
evidence: Supported by cocaine toxicity data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: NIC offspring are hyper-responsive to multiple xenobiotics.
source: Astonishingly, this acclimation protocol resulted in enhanced resistance to cocaine toxicity in NIC offspring, relative to TA controls (Figure 5B), revealing that NIC offspring are hyper-responsive to multiple xenobiotics.
evidence: Inferred from enhanced resistance to both nicotine and cocaine.

claim: Pre-acclimation to nicotine induced a cocaine-resistant phenotype in NIC offspring.
source: Consistent with the hypothesis that drug acclimation induces a general xenobiotic response, we found that pre-acclimation to nicotine induced a cocaine-resistant phenotype in NIC offspring, and, conversely, that chronic cocaine could induce nicotine resistance (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: Supported by cross-drug toxicity data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Chronic cocaine could induce nicotine resistance in NIC offspring.
source: Consistent with the hypothesis that drug acclimation induces a general xenobiotic response, we found that pre-acclimation to nicotine induced a cocaine-resistant phenotype in NIC offspring, and, conversely, that chronic cocaine could induce nicotine resistance (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: Supported by cross-drug toxicity data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Paternal nicotine exposure programs a hyper-responsive state in male offspring in which chronic xenobiotic exposure results in generalized toxin resistance.
source: Together, these data suggest that paternal nicotine exposure programs a hyper-responsive state in male offspring in which chronic xenobiotic exposure results in a generalized toxin resistance.
evidence: Concluded from the cross-drug resistance experiments.

claim: Mecamylamine administration prevents nicotine-induced anorexia.
source: Studies have previously shown that mecamylamine administration prevents known physiological responses to nicotine such as nicotine-induced anorexia (Mineur et al., 2011), hypothermia and locomotor effects (Tapper et al., 2004), and nicotine reinforcement (Corrigall and Coen, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mineur et al., 2011.

claim: Mecamylamine administration prevents nicotine-induced hypothermia and locomotor effects.
source: Studies have previously shown that mecamylamine administration prevents known physiological responses to nicotine such as nicotine-induced anorexia (Mineur et al., 2011), hypothermia and locomotor effects (Tapper et al., 2004), and nicotine reinforcement (Corrigall and Coen, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tapper et al., 2004.

claim: Mecamylamine administration prevents nicotine reinforcement.
source: Studies have previously shown that mecamylamine administration prevents known physiological responses to nicotine such as nicotine-induced anorexia (Mineur et al., 2011), hypothermia and locomotor effects (Tapper et al., 2004), and nicotine reinforcement (Corrigall and Coen, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation to Corrigall and Coen, 1989.

claim: Male mice concurrently treated with nicotine and mecamylamine fathered offspring with enhanced nicotine resistance.
source: Surprisingly, male mice concurrently treated with nicotine and its antagonist fathered offspring with the same enhanced nicotine resistance seen in NIC offspring (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The nicotine exposure paradigm does not induce paternal effects on offspring as a consequence of nicotine withdrawal stress.
source: Importantly, this finding rigorously rules out the possibility that our nicotine exposure paradigm induces paternal effects on offspring as a consequence of the nicotine withdrawal stress imposed in the week before mating.
evidence: Inferred from the mecamylamine experiment results.

claim: The drug resistance observed in nicotine+mecamylamine offspring argues that this paternal effect does not require nicotine signaling in treated fathers.
source: Moreover, the drug resistance observed in nicotine+mecamylamine offspring strongly argues that this paternal effect does not even require nicotine signaling in treated fathers, instead suggesting that the paternal effect is perhaps induced simply by exposure to xenobiotics.
evidence: Inferred from the mecamylamine experiment results.

claim: Mecamylamine exposure alone induced drug resistance in the next generation.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, mecamylamine exposure alone also induced drug resistance in the next generation, although this effect was not as robust as that induced by nicotine or nicotine+mecamylamine (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Drug resistance in sons can be induced by paternal exposure to both nAChR agonists and nAChR antagonists.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that drug resistance in sons can be induced by paternal exposure to both nAChR agonists and nAChR antagonists, arguing that paternal xenobiotic exposure is likely to be the relevant feature of our nicotine exposure paradigm.
evidence: Concluded from the mecamylamine experiments.

claim: Paternal xenobiotic exposure is likely to be the relevant feature of the nicotine exposure paradigm for inducing offspring drug resistance.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that drug resistance in sons can be induced by paternal exposure to both nAChR agonists and nAChR antagonists, arguing that paternal xenobiotic exposure is likely to be the relevant feature of our nicotine exposure paradigm.
evidence: Inferred from the mecamylamine experiments showing both agonists and antagonists induce the effect.

claim: Hepatocyte apoptosis and necrosis were extremely common in livers from cocaine-exposed TA offspring.
source: Importantly, while hepatocyte apoptosis and necrosis were extremely common in livers from cocaine-exposed TA offspring, NIC offspring were significantly protected from such cocaine toxicity (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 7.

claim: NIC offspring were significantly protected from cocaine-induced hepatocyte apoptosis and necrosis.
source: Importantly, while hepatocyte apoptosis and necrosis were extremely common in livers from cocaine-exposed TA offspring, NIC offspring were significantly protected from such cocaine toxicity (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The upregulation of xenobiotic processing genes in naïve NIC offspring is not sufficient to significantly protect animals from a lethal nicotine or cocaine challenge.
source: We conclude that the upregulation of XPGs in naïve NIC offspring is not sufficient to significantly protect animals from a lethal nicotine or cocaine challenge, but that this upregulation can protect hepatocytes from sub-lethal doses of these drugs.
evidence: Concluded from the combination of gene expression data and toxicity assays.

claim: The upregulation of xenobiotic processing genes in NIC offspring can protect hepatocytes from sub-lethal doses of drugs.
source: We conclude that the upregulation of XPGs in naïve NIC offspring is not sufficient to significantly protect animals from a lethal nicotine or cocaine challenge, but that this upregulation can protect hepatocytes from sub-lethal doses of these drugs.
evidence: Concluded from the hepatocyte viability data.

claim: Following chronic toxin exposure, TA offspring are left with substantially reduced liver function while NIC offspring maintain greater numbers of functional hepatocytes.
source: Following a week of chronic toxin exposure, TA offspring are left with substantially reduced liver function, while NIC offspring maintain greater numbers of functional hepatocytes.
evidence: Inferred from the hepatocyte viability data.

claim: Greater hepatocyte functional capacity and upregulation of xenobiotic processing genes may both protect NIC animals from a single toxic dose of xenobiotic.
source: We speculate that this greater hepatocyte functional capacity, as well as the upregulation of XPGs in hepatocytes (Figure 4), may both serve to protect the animal from a single toxic dose of xenobiotic.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of protection.

claim: Paternal nicotine exposure induces a pleiotropic set of phenotypes in male offspring.
source: Taken together, our data reveal (1) that paternal nicotine exposure induces a pleiotropic set of phenotypes in male offspring, and (2) that the induced phenotypes in offspring are not specific for nicotine.
evidence: Concluded from the multiple phenotypes observed including drug resistance and metabolic changes.

claim: The induced phenotypes in offspring are not specific for nicotine.
source: Taken together, our data reveal (1) that paternal nicotine exposure induces a pleiotropic set of phenotypes in male offspring, and (2) that the induced phenotypes in offspring are not specific for nicotine.
evidence: Concluded from the cross-drug resistance experiments.

claim: Paternal nicotine exposure only affects drug resistance in male offspring.
source: Here, we find that paternal nicotine exposure only affects drug resistance in male offspring, raising once again the unsolved question of why paternal environments induce gender-specific outcomes in progeny.
evidence: Supported by the lack of effect in female offspring in toxicity assays.

claim: NIC offspring exhibited significantly diminished clearance of a glucose bolus.
source: Consistent with the ability of multiple paternal environments to alter glucose control in offspring, we observed that NIC offspring exhibited significantly diminished clearance of a glucose bolus, as well as a moderately diminished response to insulin.
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: NIC offspring exhibited a moderately diminished response to insulin.
source: Consistent with the ability of multiple paternal environments to alter glucose control in offspring, we observed that NIC offspring exhibited significantly diminished clearance of a glucose bolus, as well as a moderately diminished response to insulin.
evidence: Supported by insulin tolerance test data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The drug-resistant state in NIC offspring is only revealed by pre-exposure of these animals to xenobiotics.
source: A crucial feature of the drug resistance exhibited by NIC offspring is that the toxin-resistant state is only revealed by pre-exposure of these animals to xenobiotics.
evidence: Concluded from the difference between naïve and chronic challenge experiments.

claim: The development of an animal's phenotype involves an interaction between environmental conditions in two consecutive generations.
source: This requirement for drug pre-exposure/acclimation emphasizes the key role of the offspring's environment in the manifestation of an epigenetically 'reprogrammed' phenotype. In other words, the development of an animal's phenotype here involves an interaction between environmental conditions in two consecutive generations (see (Rodgers et al., 2013; Zeybel et al., 2012) for similar examples) – as with gene X environment effects, epigenetic marks also have context-dependent effects on organismal phenotype.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the requirement for drug acclimation to reveal the phenotype.

claim: Epigenetic marks have context-dependent effects on organismal phenotype.
source: This requirement for drug pre-exposure/acclimation emphasizes the key role of the offspring's environment in the manifestation of an epigenetically 'reprogrammed' phenotype. In other words, the development of an animal's phenotype here involves an interaction between environmental conditions in two consecutive generations (see (Rodgers et al., 2013; Zeybel et al., 2012) for similar examples) – as with gene X environment effects, epigenetic marks also have context-dependent effects on organismal phenotype.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the requirement for drug acclimation.

claim: Paternal nicotine exposure does not affect anxiety-related behavior in offspring.
source: Second, in contrast to multiple reported paternal stress paradigms, we do not find any evidence that paternal nicotine exposure affects anxiety-related behavior in offspring (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by anxiety assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: CAR and PXR represent appealing candidates for the relevant xenobiotic sensor in fathers.
source: As a diverse variety of xenobiotics can affect gene regulation via activation of the NHRs CAR and PXR, these NHRs represent appealing candidates for the relevant xenobiotic sensor in fathers.
evidence: This is speculation based on known functions of CAR and PXR.

claim: Nicotine acts by binding to and activating nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
source: Nicotine is a commonly-used drug in humans, and acts by binding to and activating nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs), ligand-gated cation channels normally activated by the endogenous neurotransmitter acetylcholine.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nicotine's mechanism of action.

claim: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are ligand-gated cation channels normally activated by acetylcholine.

claim: The liver is the primary site of nicotine and other xenobiotic clearance in mammals.
source: As the liver is the primary site of nicotine and other xenobiotic clearance in mammals, we investigated changes in mRNA abundance in hepatocytes isolated from TA and NIC offspring (Figure 4B–C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is established knowledge about hepatic function.

claim: Normalized ATAC peaks at regulatory elements were nearly 2-fold higher in NIC hepatocytes than in TA hepatocytes.
source: Comparing TA and NIC datasets, we observed a consistent global difference in overall chromatin accessibility – normalized ATAC peaks at regulatory elements were nearly 2-fold higher in NIC hepatocytes than in TA hepatocytes, while TA hepatocytes exhibited a consistently higher background of transposition throughout regions of the genome distant from regulatory elements (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-Seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.
